issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: 'Listening for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home' implies a home-intrusion/assault threat script. For a terrorism trauma in a combat pilot, this is not impossible, but it is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile because no other items indicate a home-invasion-type trauma context.

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is more typically linked to sexual assault or interpersonal violation. In this profile it does not fit well with terrorism trauma and is not supported by the other selected triggers, threat, or strategy items.

issues.item: Male Presence: Being alone with men
issues.explanation: 'Being alone with men' as a trigger suggests an interpersonal male-perpetrator association. That conflicts with the stated terrorism trauma unless there was an additional gendered assault component, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

vignette:
Claire Martin is a 45-year-old American combat pilot who came to treatment after months of telling herself that what happened “could have been worse,” even as her life had narrowed around fear. During a deployment-related transit through a civilian airport, she was caught in a terrorist bombing. She had been moving through a crowded terminal when the blast went off nearby. What she remembers most sharply is the compression of bodies as people surged in every direction, the sudden crushing press of strangers against her, the violent noise, and then the choking sense that there was nowhere to go. For several moments she was pinned between luggage barriers and other passengers, half crouched, half shoved forward, with alarms blaring and people screaming over one another. Smoke and dust filled the air. She recalls the sickly wave in her stomach, the metallic taste in her mouth, and the immediate conviction that another explosion could come at any second.

In the days afterward, Claire returned to duty and spoke about the event in the brisk, minimizing way that had long served her in military life. She told herself she had survived, other people had not, and that dwelling on it would be self-indulgent. That comparison became a familiar refrain: it could have been worse, so she should be able to carry on. Yet her reactions did not settle. Loud noises began to hit her with a force she found difficult to hide. A slammed door in a hangar, an engine backfire on base, even the sharp clatter of equipment being dropped could make her whole body jolt before she had time to think. In those moments she felt as if she were back in the terminal at the instant of the blast, her body already braced for impact.

Crowded settings became especially difficult. The base cafeteria at lunch, airport security lines, even busy grocery store aisles felt intolerable because she could feel people closing in around her. She became acutely aware of exits, bottlenecks, and anyone moving too quickly nearby. If she could not keep space around herself, she felt trapped. She started avoiding enclosed or confined spaces whenever she could, taking stairs instead of elevators, stepping out of packed briefing rooms, and lingering near doorways during meetings. As a combat pilot, much of her work required disciplined focus in restricted, highly controlled spaces, and she began to notice how much effort it took to manage herself before and after those situations. She was not describing fear of flying; rather, it was the sense of confinement and blocked escape in ordinary parts of the workday that wore her down. She would arrive early so she could choose a seat near the exit, or wait until others had cleared out before entering a narrow operations room.

She also became more watchful in ways that felt excessive even to her. Walking across parking lots or through transit areas, she repeatedly looked behind her to check whether anyone was following. She scanned faces, listened for abrupt changes in noise, and tracked where people were standing. At night she had trouble falling asleep and often woke again after only a few hours, alert and listening. Fatigue made her feel physically off, and feeling physically unwell had become a trigger in its own right. If she noticed nausea, dizziness, or the heaviness of coming down with something, her mind jumped back to the bodily sensations she remembered before and after the explosion. A simple virus or dehydration could spiral quickly into the feeling that something terrible was about to happen.

Over time Claire had come to believe that she could no longer deal with even minor upsets. A scheduling change, a crowded waiting area, a sudden noise that another person would brush off could leave her feeling unsteady for hours. What frightened her most was not only the reactions themselves but what they seemed to mean. She was certain the world was dangerous in a way she had once understood abstractly and now felt everywhere, in airports, stores, public streets, anywhere people gathered. Alongside that was a bleak sense of helplessness: bad things happened without warning, and she could not stop them. Smoking became one of the few things she used to steady herself between tasks, during breaks, and after encounters she knew would be difficult.

She finally sought help after a recent work trip routed her through another busy airport. By the time she reached the terminal gate area, hemmed in by lines of passengers and punctuated announcements, she was already scanning constantly and looking over her shoulder. When a loud noise echoed from nearby construction, she froze, then left the area to stand outside despite the inconvenience and professional embarrassment. She told the therapist she was tired of organizing her life around exits, open space, cigarettes, and the hope that nothing would set her off. At the same time, she was afraid that treatment might force her to face how little control she feels she has, and she said what she wants most is to move through the world—and through her job—without being so certain that danger is always about to break open around her.
